Well, technically it doesn't have to have a Gaussian distribution (bell-shape) - it could be skewed to one or other end. It is, however, a property of polygenic/multifactorial inheritance that distribution of phenotype resembles a Gaussian distribution. The more genes involved, the less discrete the distribution (a mathematician might be able to phrase that better for me). The distribution of IQs could be used as a heuristic to correctly argue that intelligence is multifactorial. By extension, you could ask your question of any multifactorial inheritable characteristic (e.g. height).

Simplifying the scenario somewhat (read: a lot) you could imagine that there are a series of genes for intelligence, each with two alleles: one being the stupid allele and one being the smart allele; they are effectively binary switches. Imagine two potential parents with 50% of their switches in the on position, each (for simplicity you could imagine them as a haploid organism and extend this to diploidy when you're comfortable). When they breed, their offspring will receive a random assortment of switches from each parent, constituting 50% of that parent's switches. The most probable outcome is that they will receive these switches in the same proportion as the parents: 50% on, 50% off. There is, however, a lesser probability that they will receive other combinations of on/off (the greater the combination varies from 50-50, the less the probability). You will find if you do the analysis that this gives you a Gaussian distribution.

My Oranda and first Dojo moved over 1500 miles from Southern California :)

Get some big buckets, mine were transported in a 5gal bucket that we had rigged with a battery powered air pump. So there's that option, just be sure to keep them covered up.

I will agree with longlostbleu on the buckets and battery powered bubbler. When I've transported fish over long distances, I have used buckets and Totes depending on the distance I was moving. A few things to do to prep.
1) Don't feed your fish for 24-48 hours prior to move.
2) In the week leading up to the moved, do 2 or 3 20% water change during that last week, so the water is free of any high levels ammonia or nitrites.
3) unless you are going to rig up a power inverter and throw a heater in with them, the temp will drop as you transport them. It's best to lower the temp in the tank a day or two before the move for the following reason. 1. lower temp water allows higher oxygen content in the water. 2. lower temps slows the metabolize of the fish and so they aren't as energetic and so don't consume the oxygen as fast as they would if they where active. 3. Cooler water means that their won't be as much of a temperature swing during the trip. (remember science class. The hot a liquid is, the faster it cools.)
4) whether you bag, bucket,or tote them, leave 2/3 air and 1/3 water so it takes longer for the oxygen to be depleted. Look at the size of your fish and determine the appropriate size container.
5) insulate whatever they are going in as best as possible. but them in a syrofoam cooler, or a bucket with a blanked wrapped around it. Anything that will slow the temperature dropping below unsafe levels. Remember that Tropical fish can easily tolerate 66-68 degree temperatures for up to a few days. If you have them in the car with you, don't blast the A/C lower than 68.
6) Some people put a few drops of prime into the water before they seal up the container/bag. This isn't a bad suggestion as the whole experience will be stressful and might bring on a sickness that your fish wouldn't have gotten had they not been stressed.
7) if you stop and check on the fish and see that they are gasping for air. If they are in a bag, open it up and compress all the air out of it and then open it back up and reseal it. Refrain from blowing in it as you are only expelling Co2 and it won't help. If they are in a container with a lid, take the lid of and fan it a cross the top to draw off the air inside and replace with outside air.
8) open the containers as little as possible if the container isn't climate controlled. If they are in the care, that is fine. If they are in the trailer or truck, than opening the container will release some of the warmth which will drop the water temp.
I can't think of anything else off hand other than to either drip or float acclimate them once they get to the new home.
